transcript.en: But then there are some elements that you talk about, like yttrium, which some are calling the killer choke point because diversification from that would actually take years. Yttrium is used in lasers, some advanced ceramics, and in some superconducting materials.
transcript.zh: 但你在文中也提到了一些关键元素，比如钇，有人称其为“杀手级卡脖子点”，因为针对它的替代和多元化需要耗费数年时间。钇被广泛应用于激光、部分先进陶瓷材料以及某些超导材料中。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Gloria, from the Chinese side, where do China's own experts think that their leverage is really deep, and where do they think it's actually kind of thin? Do they seem to see the same limits that you assess?
transcript.zh: Gloria，从中国方面来看，中国自己的专家认为他们真正的杀手锏在哪里？在哪些方面筹码其实比较有限？他们眼中的局限性与你的评估一致吗？

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: I think regarding the leverage that China has in this area, I don't see a huge gap in perception. China still dominates mining and midstream processing and separation of rare earths, especially when it comes to technically difficult separation of heavy rare earths.
transcript.zh: 我认为关于中国在这一领域的筹码优势，双方的认知并没有太大差距。中国在稀土开采、中游加工以及分离技术上依然占据绝对主导地位，特别是在技术难度极高的重稀土分离领域。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: What may surprise...
transcript.zh: 可能让人感到意外的是……

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Many is that this narrative of impending depletion of China's rare earth material, it started to prevail in in Chinese public discussion and also policy discussion as well almost two decades ago.
transcript.zh: 很多人的看法是，关于中国稀土资源即将枯竭的叙事，早在近二十年前就已开始在中国公众舆论和政策讨论中占据主流。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Part of it is because, you know, all of these resources, whether it's rare earths or critical minerals, are non-renewable in nature. Part of it is also, I think, because Chinese experts themselves see high dependence on overseas imports for several critical minerals, such as lithium and nickel.
transcript.zh: 部分原因在于，这些资源——无论是稀土还是关键矿产——本质上都是不可再生的。我认为另一部分原因在于，中国专家自己也看到了在锂、镍等若干关键矿产上对海外进口的高度依赖。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: So, I mean, they worry that in the future, China would become dependent on foreign imports and they can be used as chokepoints against China. So, I think this high level of resource insecurity despite its dominance is critical to keep in mind.
transcript.zh: 因此，他们担忧未来中国会变得依赖外国进口，而这些领域可能会被用来对中国实施“卡脖子”。所以，我认为必须牢记的是：尽管中国拥有主导地位，但其内部却存在着极高的资源不安全感。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Another hidden vulnerability is its insufficient control over advanced high-tech applications, so those high-value downstream functional material. I remember there's this one book published maybe a few months ago, the authors noted that China's still playing catch-up to the US and Japan when it comes to high-end downstream patents.
transcript.zh: 另一个隐藏的脆弱点在于，中国对尖端高科技应用的掌控不足，也就是那些高附加值的下游功能性材料。我记得几个月前出版的一本书中，作者指出在高价值的下游专利方面，中国仍在努力追赶美国和日本。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: So, I think, you know, this is a good point to emphasize that even in this one single sector of rare earths, we still see a level of interdependence in in some ways.
transcript.zh: 所以我觉得，这很能说明问题：即使仅就稀土这一个单一行业而言，我们在某些维度上仍能看到某种程度的相互依存。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So, Gloria, staying with you, let's go back to the Chinese domestic picture as it stands right now. So, the industry, you know, has gone from these artisanal mines and the crime rings that you guys talked about with like all the acid rain, to now what is it, like six state groups in 2014 to now these two national champions today in 2025.
transcript.zh: 那么 Gloria，继续问你，让我们回到目前中国国内的现状。这个行业经历了从你们提到的手工小作坊、伴随严重酸雨的犯罪团伙，到 2014 年整合为六家国有集团，再到如今 2025 年形成的两大“国家队”龙头企业。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Has the Wild West finally been tamed? Do the local governments that used to resist Beijing for decades, do they finally, you know, obey central directives?
transcript.zh: 这片“荒野西部”最终被驯服了吗？那些曾对抗北京数十年的地方政府，现在是否终于听从中央指令了呢？

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: I would say partially. One of the stated goals of consolidating this industry, at least in official narrative, is to improve environmental standards. So, cracking down on unlicensed mining certainly helped with the environmental fallout. Historically, the most severe environmental pollution took place at those illegal mines.
transcript.zh: 我认为只能说部分做到了。至少在官方叙事中，整合该行业的既定目标之一就是提高环保标准。因此，打击无证开采确实减轻了环境破坏。从历史上看，最严重的环境污染正是发生在那些非法矿井中。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: When it comes to pollution oversight, I would argue that it's always this cycle of crackdown and then ease up and crack down again, so enforcement gap will, in some way, inevitably always show up. And another interesting contradiction is that, besides the geopolitical tensions...
transcript.zh: 但在污染监管方面，我认为一直存在“先严打、后放松、再严打”的循环，因此执行缺口在某种程度上总会不可避免地出现。另一个耐人寻味的矛盾在于，除了地缘政治紧张局势之外……

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Which everyone is talking about. The strategic importance of rare earth materials was elevated since 2020 also because of China's clean energy drive.
transcript.zh: 大家都在讨论这个问题。自2020年以来，稀土材料的战略重要性显著提升，这也源于中国对清洁能源的大力推动。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Since these elements are indispensable for manufacturing whether it's EV motors or wind turbines. So you do have right now this contradiction that producing rare earths are polluting, but also China is striving to be a green tech giant.
transcript.zh: 因为制造新能源汽车电机或风力发电机，都离不开这些元素。因此，目前确实存在这样一种矛盾：稀土生产伴随着高污染，但同时中国又致力于成为绿色科技巨头。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Is it just the focus? I mean, because I wonder has the whole political economy of rare earths in China, has it now been fully securitized or are there still sort of commercial or provincial interests that pull against this sort of framing of rare earths as just a weaponized resource?
transcript.zh: 这只是关注重点的不同吗？我的意思是，我想知道中国稀土的整个政治经济格局，现在是已经完全被泛安全化了，还是依然存在某些商业或地方省份的利益，在抗衡这种单纯把稀土当成武器化资源的定性？

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: At this point, as you mentioned Kaiser, we've seen the industry consolidating around two national champions. So, in terms of industrial structure, it's no longer fragmented, right? There is tighter central oversight.
transcript.zh: 眼下，正如 Kaiser 你所提到的，我们看到该产业已经整合到两大国家队领头羊企业麾下。因此，从产业结构来看，它不再是一盘散沙，确实有了更严格的中央监管。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Yeah. But just like in any other sectors in China, local interest and imperative would always persist. I mean, the way they're incentivized differently on tax revenue and resource allocation, it isn't random. It's built into the system.
transcript.zh: 是的。但就像中国的任何其他行业一样，地方利益和诉求永远存在。我的意思是，他们在税收和资源配置上受到的激励机制截然不同，这并非偶然，而是根植于体制之中的。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: And for anyone who is interested in this sub-national dynamic should read this China Quarterly article written by Jessica DiCarlo, Kooroshy, and Rafael Dabert. This is one of the most consequential piece that I've read on China's rare earth industry.
transcript.zh: 任何对这种地方动态感兴趣的人，都应该读一读 Jessica DiCarlo、Corey Com 与 Rafael Dabert 在《中国季刊》（China Quarterly）上发表的那篇文章。这是我读过的关于中国稀土产业最具分量的论文之一。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: According to them, they describe this central-local relationship as fractured. So, it's not wholly centralized, but also not that fragmented as it was before.
transcript.zh: 据他们的分析，这种央地关系被描述为“断裂性”的（fractured）。也就是说，它既没有完全集权化，也不像以前那样彻底碎片化。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: I would just add one Chinese idiom saying that for every policy from above, there is always a countermeasure from below. So, I think that's what we're seeing in the rare earth industry as well.
transcript.zh: 我想引用一句中国老话：“上有政策，下有对策”。我认为在稀土行业，我们同样看到了这种情况。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: There's always going to be some, you know, local selective enforcement of central directives.
transcript.zh: 地方上在执行中央政令时，总归会存在某种选择性执法的现象。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So, I want to wrap up here by asking about, you know, what our prescriptions are. And maybe if I'm reading you correctly, your prescriptions, Jessica, is reciprocal de-escalation, deterrence.
transcript.zh: 在节目的最后，我想探讨一下你们开出的政策药方。Jessica，如果我理解得没错的话，你的建议是对等的缓和与威慑。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: The part that will be hardest to sell in Washington is positive reciprocity, right? Encouraging bilateral trade and investment, joint ventures and licensing of Chinese technology in areas like batteries so American firms can compete alongside China.
transcript.zh: 而在华盛顿最难推销的部分，莫过于“积极互惠”（positive reciprocity），对吧？也就是鼓励双边贸易与投资、成立合资企业，以及在电池等领域对中国技术进行授权许可，从而让美国企业能够与中国并肩竞争。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: This is—these are your words: alongside China, not only against it. You cite, like, Financial Times estimate that fully...
transcript.zh: 这是你原话：与中国“并肩”（alongside），而不仅仅是与中国“对抗”（against）。你引用了诸如《金融时报》的估算，称要完全……

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: ...that getting the US out of Chinese supply chains would cost something like $13 trillion over 25 years. And then there's, you know, your former co-author Tom Christensen's argument, which I think is, you know, your most strategically important point, that if Beijing comes to believe US markets will be cut off unconditionally, Washington just loses the coercive leverage that it's always felt it needs to deter something like, you know, a Chinese move against Taiwan.
transcript.zh: ……让美国彻底摆脱中国供应链，在未来25年内将耗费约13万亿美元。此外，还有你之前的合作作者Tom Christensen的观点——我认为这是你们最具战略意义的核心论点：如果北京认定无论如何都会被彻底切断与美国市场的联系，那么华盛顿就会丧失一直以来赖以慑止中国对台采取行动的强制性筹码。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So, given where the politics are, you know, where you've got like even something like a Ford and CATL licensing deal, where it becomes kind of a congressional scandal, what does positive reciprocity look like in practice? What's the version of this that could actually survive this post-midterm House?
transcript.zh: 那么，考虑到当前的政治现实——哪怕是福特（Ford）与宁德时代（CATL）之间的技术许可合作，都会演变成国会层面的政治丑闻——在现实中，“积极对等”究竟该如何落地？在如今的中期选举后众议院格局下，到底什么样的方案才具有真正的生存空间？

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: So, I think there are a lot of different ways that positive reciprocity could play out if both Beijing and Washington would allow it. We've just talked about investment, and I recommend the UCSD report on selective openness, there was a piece by Peter Cowhey and Nick Lardy talking about how existing screening mechanisms could be strengthened, but ultimately at the end of the day, the United States would benefit by allowing in Chinese technology and licensing, in an effort to stand up American competitiveness in many of these industries where China leads.
transcript.zh: 我认为，如果北京和华盛顿都放行，积极对等可以通过很多不同的方式展开。我们刚才讨论了投资，我推荐加州大学圣地亚哥分校（UCSD）关于“选择性开放”的报告，Peter Cowhey等人曾撰文探讨如何强化现有的审查机制，但归根结底，允许引进中国技术与技术许可，将有助于提升美国在许多中国领跑产业中的自身竞争力，美国最终将从中受益。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: There's other areas of positive reciprocity. I would point to, for example, making progress on reducing the tensions that prevent more exchange of students, scholars, people, right? You have indications at the presidential level, anyway, that these are welcome, but the actual policies are going in the opposite direction and making it harder and creating a broader chilling effect on that exchange.
transcript.zh: 在积极对等层面还有其他领域。比如，努力缓解阻碍学生、学者以及民间交流进一步扩大的紧张局势。至少在总统层面已有表态欢迎这些交流，但实际政策却背道而驰，不仅设置了更多阻碍，还对人文交流产生了更广泛的寒蝉效应。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: I would think that even on the issue of Taiwan, Trump has made a number of remarks that have been welcomed in Beijing, but it's not clear to me that he's gotten anything from it. And I don't mean here trade concessions, I mean a reciprocal pullback of Chinese military operations around Taiwan.
transcript.zh: 我认为即便在台湾问题上，特朗普总统虽然发表过一些受到北京欢迎的言论，但我看不出他从中换取到了什么实质筹码。我指的不是贸易上的让步，而是指中国大陆在台湾周边的军事行动能够相应有所收敛。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: And so, I think we need to think a little bit less unilaterally and more reciprocally, so that, as we show, there's an action-reaction spiral in a dangerous direction. And maybe it has slowed somewhat under this administration, Trump 2.0, post the Busan Summit. But whether that will be extended, I think, really requires all of us to understand that there is going to be no winning, ultimately, and that we actually just need to manage this interdependence.
transcript.zh: 因此，我认为我们需要少一点单边思维，多一点对等考量。正如我们指出的，双方之间存在着滑向危险方向的“行动-反应”螺旋。在釜山峰会之后的特朗普2.0政府任内，这种势头或许有所放缓。但这种缓和能否维系，归根结底取决于我们所有人能否认识到：这场博弈根本不可能有赢家，我们实际上必须学会妥善管理这种相互依存关系。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: Which does require, you know, defeating hubris on the other side, so some degree of diversification is necessary to avoid these easily exploitable chokepoints. But we also need to recognize that continued integration, interdependence is actually a source of stability and not just potential weaponization.
transcript.zh: 这当然需要打掉对方的傲慢，因此适度的多元化是必要的，以避免出现容易被利用的卡脖子关卡。但我们也必须认识到，持续的深度融合与相互依存实际上是稳定的基石，而不仅仅意味着潜在的武器化风险。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Gloria, everyone else gets left out of the conversation so often when we talk about rare earths, US-China, stuff like this, but...
transcript.zh: Gloria，当我们讨论稀土、中美博弈这类议题时，其他各方往往完全被排除在对话之外，但是……

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: You know, there are many countries with viable rare earth deposits that don't want to choose between China and the United States. I think about, you know, Myanmar, which is supplying a huge share of the heavy rare earth feedstocks that go into China's processors from, you know, it's a conflict zone that nobody controls.
transcript.zh: 很多拥有可开采稀土矿藏的国家，其实并不想在中美之间选边站队。我想到比如缅甸，它为中国的加工企业提供了大量的重稀土原料，而这些原料来自几乎无人能实质控制的冲突地区。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Australia and Lynas, Vietnam, Brazil, the Central African deposits that everybody is suddenly courting — again, a very war-torn area in eastern Congo especially. But Gloria, how does Beijing think about these third countries?
transcript.zh: 还有澳大利亚与莱纳斯公司（Lynas）、越南、巴西，以及各方突然竞相拉拢的中非矿藏——那同样是一个饱受战火蹂躏的地区，尤其是刚果（金）东部。那么 Gloria，北京究竟是如何看待这些第三国矿源的？

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Do they see them as territory to lock up, or as a hedge that makes its own leverage more sustainable, or is it something else? I mean, does the Global South's reluctance to pick sides work in Beijing's advantage, or does it work against Beijing?
transcript.zh: 是把它们视为必须先下手锁定的地盘，还是看作一种能让自己筹码更具可持续性的对冲手段？抑或是别的考量？全球南方不愿选边站的态度，对北京来说究竟是利还是弊？

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: To answer your question here, Kaiser, I would say it's not either-or, but both-and, and the answer is really based on which third country that we're talking about, so it's more like a case-by-case. From my reading of the Chinese language resources, I think they are highly aware of the potential geopolitical risk posed by, you know, their import dependence regarding several critical minerals.
transcript.zh: 回答你的问题，Kaiser，我认为这并非二选一，而是兼而有之，而且这完全取决于我们具体讨论的是哪一个第三国，基本上是一事一议。从我查阅的中文文献来看，中国非常清楚自己在若干关键矿物上对进口的依赖所带来的潜在地缘政治风险。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: They discuss about potential political instability and frequent policy changes in those countries, in those resource-rich countries in Africa, in Latin America. For instance, I mean, they talk about the risk of civil war in Congo, and, you know, the rise of resource nationalism in those countries as well.
transcript.zh: 他们经常讨论这些国家潜在的政局动荡以及频繁的政策变动，尤其是在非洲和拉美的那些资源富集国。例如，他们会谈到刚果（金）内战的风险，以及这些国家资源民族主义抬头的趋势。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: So, I think, you know, they do perceive risk from policy change in those countries. And I think in many ways we see the security dilemma kind of spill over to US-China competition in those third countries, and as you mentioned here, many of them are not trying to stick to one side.
transcript.zh: 因此，他们确实敏锐察觉到了这些国家政策转向所带来的风险。在很多方面，我们看到这种安全困境正在外溢到中美在第三国的竞争中；正如你所言，很多第三国其实并不打算死心塌地倒向任何一方。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Well, this has been wonderful. I want to thank you both so much for taking the time to talk about this piece, again, which I highly recommend that everyone take a look at. It's in the latest edition of Foreign Affairs.
transcript.zh: 今天的讨论非常精彩。非常感谢两位抽出时间来聊这篇文章，我再次强烈推荐大家都去读一读，文章刊登在最新一期的《外交事务》（Foreign Affairs）上。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Let me also mention that Jessica has two interviews that you're going to want to listen to and read: listen to her excellent interview with Dan Kurtz-Phelan, editor of Foreign Affairs, on The Foreign Affairs Interview podcast, and also check out her interview in The Monitor, which is the newsletter of the Carter Center's US-China Perception Monitor.
transcript.zh: 另外提一句，Jessica 最近有两场非常值得收听和阅读的专访：一场是她在《外交事务访谈》播客中与主编 Dan Kurtz-Phelan 的深度对话；另一场刊登在卡特中心“中美印象”项目的简报《The Monitor》上。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: This all has me very eager to get a galley copy of Jessica's forthcoming book about what China wants, and to get her back on the show to a deep dive into that. But yeah, make sure in the meantime to read this piece.
transcript.zh: 这些都让我十分期待能早日拿到 Jessica 即将出版的关于中国意图的新书样书，届时一定会再请她回节目做深度探讨。不过眼下，大家一定要去读一读这篇文章。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: This excellent piece in Foreign Affairs. Again, the piece is called "How China Found Its Most Potent Weapon: The Real History of Beijing's Rare Earth Dominance," and the authors of course are Gloria Xiong and Jessica Chen Weiss.
transcript.zh: 《外交事务》（Foreign Affairs）上的这篇力作。再次提醒大家，这篇文章的标题是《中国如何找到其最强武器：北京稀土主导地位的真实历史》，作者正是 Gloria Xiong 和 Jessica Chen Weiss。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Let's move on now to our paying-it-forward section, where I ask each of you to name-check somebody, a younger colleague perhaps, who is doing work that you really admire, and that you think our listeners should be turned on to. Gloria, why don't you go first?
transcript.zh: 现在进入我们的“薪火相传”推荐环节。我想请两位各自推荐一位学者，也许是某位年轻同行，其研究成果令你们十分钦佩，且值得广大听众关注。Gloria，你先来吧？

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Sure. I have a few on my mind. Let me start with Wendy Leutert at Indiana University. She works on the reform and global expansion of China's state-owned enterprises.
transcript.zh: 好的。我脑海中有几位人选。先从印第安纳大学的 Wendy Leutert 说起吧。她的研究聚焦于中国国有企业的改革与全球扩张。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: She's also done terrific work with Isaac Kardon on China's investment in global ports—amazing, amazing work.
transcript.zh: 她还与 Isaac Kardon 合作开展了关于中国在全球港口投资的重磅研究，成果非常非常出色。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: I would also recommend work by Ning Leng at Georgetown University. She has recently published an award-winning book with the title Politicizing Business: How Firms Are Made to Serve the Party-State in China.
transcript.zh: 我还想推荐乔治城大学 Ning Leng 的研究。她最近出版了一本屡获殊荣的著作，书名为《将商业政治化：中国企业如何被要求服务于党国体系》（Politicizing Business: How Firms Are Made to Serve the Party-State in China）。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Last but not least is Ketian Zhang, who has written extensively on China's coercion in maritime disputes.
transcript.zh: 最后但同样重要的是 Ketian Zhang，她对中国在海洋争端中的胁迫行为进行了广泛而深入的著述。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Wow. Coercion in maritime disputes, that's a very interesting and timely topic. Fantastic! Those are three excellent ones. Jessica, can you top that?
transcript.zh: 哇，海洋争端中的胁迫行为，这确实是个非常引人入胜且切中时局的话题。太棒了！这三位都极其优秀。Jessica，你能给出更惊艳的推荐吗？

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: Let me do so. Well, first I want to acknowledge the many folks whose research that we drew on in the article. Foreign Affairs doesn't allow hyperlinks, let alone endnotes, so we really benefited from Cory Combs's research, as Gloria mentioned, on rare earths.
transcript.zh: 哈哈，我试试看。首先，我想向我们在文章中参考其研究成果的众多学者致敬。《外交事务》不提供超链接，更不用提尾注了，所以我们确实获益于 Cory Combs 的研究，正如 Gloria 刚才提到的稀土方面；

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: We would have cited the pieces by Arthur Kroeber, Henry Farrell, and Daleep Singh, if they would have allowed us to. And of course, Julie Klinger, whose pathbreaking research allowed us to dive more deeply into the narratives around 2010.
transcript.zh: 如果规则允许，我们还会引用 Arthur Kroeber、Henry Farrell 和 Daleep Singh 的文章。当然，还有 Julie Klinger，她开创性的研究让我们得以更深入地探究围绕 2010 年事件的各种叙事。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Cory Combs—if people listen to the Sinica Podcast, they're hopefully familiar also with the Trivium China podcast, which is part of the Sinica Network. Cory is a frequent guest on that along with Andrew.
transcript.zh: 提到 Cory Combs——常听 Sinica Podcast 的朋友想必对 Trivium China 播客也很熟悉，它也是 Sinica 播客网络的一部分。Cory 经常和 Andrew 一起在节目中做客。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: And he is one of the most amazing people who has just such an incredible depth of knowledge about critical minerals and about supply chains. And so, yeah, I heartily endorse your recommendation of Cory's work.
transcript.zh: 他是个极为了不起的人，对关键矿产和供应链有着令人惊叹的渊博学识。所以，是的，我由衷赞同你对 Cory 研究的推荐。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: I'd also like to acknowledge some of the work of... as you know, I'm interested in disaggregating what China wants, but I think it's also important to disaggregate what the United States wants and move that conversation beyond Washington to the many different interests of local stakeholders, and especially the cross-cutting tradeoffs that many face.
transcript.zh: 我还想提一下其他一些研究……如你所知，我一直致力于细分和解构中国究竟想要什么，但我认为同样重要的是去解构美国究竟想要什么，并将讨论从华盛顿延伸到地方利益相关者的多元诉求，尤其是许多人所面临的交错权衡。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: So this is a new project that we're going to be undertaking, and in that space, I think there's some really excellent work being done by Jack Zhang, who runs the Trade War Lab at the University of Kansas.
transcript.zh: 这是我们即将启动的一个新项目。在这一领域，我认为堪萨斯大学主持贸易战实验室（Trade War Lab）的 Jack Zhang 正在做非常出色的工作。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: And also that of Kyle Jaros and Sara Newland, who are writing a book on subnational economic statecraft.
transcript.zh: 还有 Kyle Jaros 和 Sara Newland，他们正在撰写一本关于地方层面经济治国方略（subnational economic statecraft）的专著。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: So, I highly recommend their work as well, which has inspired a lot of my thinking in this space.
transcript.zh: 所以，我也非常推荐他们的研究，这给我在该领域的很多思考带来了启发。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Fantastic. Thank you guys both for these excellent recommendations. And now on to the recommendations section where I ask you guys to talk about a book or, you know, some music, or a film that you've seen recently that you want to draw to the attention of my listeners. What you got for us? Gloria, why don't you go first?
transcript.zh: 太棒了。感谢两位带来的精彩推荐。现在进入我们节目的常规推荐环节，我想请两位分享最近读过的一本书、听过的一些音乐，或者看过的某部电影，推荐给我们的听众。你们带来了什么？Gloria，不如你先来？

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: So, this is a book that I am not reading it for the first time, but a book that I read for my first-year writing seminar in college, and as I am now returning back to classroom, it came back to mind. The book is called "Healing the Heart of Democracy" written by Parker Palmer.
transcript.zh: 我要推荐的这本书并不是我第一次读，而是在大学一年级写作研讨课上读过的。现在我重返讲台教书，它又浮现在我的脑海中。这本书叫《Healing the Heart of Democracy》，作者是 Parker Palmer。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: I think a lot of the issue that we are facing as a society, as a nation, should not only be analyzed through the lens of policy or institution—I mean, as political scientists, we enjoy doing that—but I think it should also be understood as a community and as individuals. So, yep, "Healing the Heart of Democracy."
transcript.zh: 我认为，作为一个社会、一个国家，我们面临的许多问题不仅应该从政策或制度的视角去剖析——当然，作为政治学者我们很喜欢这样做——但我认为它也应该从社群和个体的维度去理解。所以，是的，推荐《Healing the Heart of Democracy》。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Oh yeah, he is a great educator.
transcript.zh: 是的，他是一位非常了不起的教育家。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: "Healing the Heart of Democracy" by Parker Palmer, wow. I have not heard of this book. I'm going to put it in my list right away. Fantastic. There's a heart that badly needs healing right now, that's for sure.
transcript.zh: Parker Palmer 写的《Healing the Heart of Democracy》，哇。我以前还没听说过这本书。我得马上把它加入我的书单。太棒了。当下确实有一颗极需疗愈的“心”，这一点毫无疑问。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Oh yeah, he is a great educator.
transcript.zh: 对，他真是一位伟大的教育家。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Oh, fantastic.
transcript.zh: 太好了。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: I'll recommend two books. One is "The Scientist and the Spy" by Mara Hvistendahl.
transcript.zh: 我推荐两本书。一本是 Mara Hvistendahl 写的《The Scientist and the Spy》。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Ah, wonderful. I've had her on the show to talk about it. It's a great book, yeah.
transcript.zh: 啊，太棒了。我之前请她上过节目专门聊过这本书。确实是一本好书。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: It's a part of that I use to conclude my seminar that I teach at SAIS on perspectives and debates on Chinese foreign policy. And you know, I think ultimately for me, it's that, you know, while there may be nefarious activities that Beijing or Chinese actors are undertaking, it's really critical that we don't lose sight of the issue of proportionality.
transcript.zh: 我在约翰斯·霍普金斯大学保罗·尼采高级国际研究学院（SAIS）讲授一门关于中国对外政策视角与辩论的研讨课，常借用这本书的内容作结。对我来说，其核心在于：尽管北京或某些中方参与者可能确实存在一些恶意行径，但我们切不可忽视按比例应对这一原则。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: That in our overreaction, that we don't actually undo the things or contribute to the further destruction of American civil liberties, democratic norms, and those legal process.
transcript.zh: 我们不能在过度反应中，亲手毁掉那些基石，或者进一步侵蚀美国的公民自由、民主规范以及合法的司法程序。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Amen.
transcript.zh: 说得太对了。

transcript.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
transcript.en: Also recommend "The Whistlers" by Ann Patchett, a work of fiction, but a beautiful, I think, reminder of what we inspire in each other.
transcript.zh: 另外我还推荐 Ann Patchett 的虚构小说《Whistler》，这是一部非常优美的小说，提醒我们人与人之间如何相互激发与启迪。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Fantastic. I have, as I've said in the last couple of shows, I am at the very end—actually tomorrow it expires—my moratorium on reading any non-fiction for the summer. So I'm going to predictably plug another novel.
transcript.zh: 太棒了。正如我在过去几期节目里提到的，我给自己定下的“夏季禁读非虚构作品”的期限马上就要结束了——其实明天就到期了。所以不出所料，我又要推荐一部小说了。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Actually, I plugged it on the last show, and I mean the author, Wallace Stegner. This time it's his novel "Angle of Repose," which actually won the Pulitzer in 1972. And I'd somehow never read it, but it turns out to be actually, to tie it to today's conversation, kind of about mining, a little bit anyway. The setup of it is there's a retired...
transcript.zh: 其实我上期节目就提过，我是说这位作者 Wallace Stegner。这次要推荐的是他的小说《Angle of Repose》（安歇角），该书曾在1972年斩获普利策奖。不知为何我以前一直没读过，但巧合的是，它恰好能呼应我们今天的讨论，里面多多少少涉及了一些采矿的内容。小说的设定是，有一位退休的……

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: historian, guy by the name of Lyman Ward. He's confined to a wheelchair, and he sets out to reconstruct the life of his grandmother, who is really larger-than-life, a woman named Susan Burling Ward, who is a real genteel eastern illustrator and fiction writer, who follows her engineer husband, this really kind of rugged, very, you know, taciturn and and very serious man, to the mining camps of the West in the 1870s and 1880s.
transcript.zh: 历史学家，名叫莱曼·沃德。他困于轮椅之上，着手重构自己祖母的一生。那是一个真正不凡的女性，名叫苏珊·伯林·沃德，是一位来自东部、温文尔雅的插画家兼小说作者，她在1870和1880年代跟随她那位坚毅粗犷、寡言少语且极为严肃的工程师丈夫，远赴西部的各个矿区营地。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So she's living in, you know, Leadville, Colorado, and in Boise, in the canyon of the Snake River, and all these places. But she never stops kind of mourning her, the civilized life in the East Coast that she's left behind.
transcript.zh: 所以她辗转生活于科罗拉多州的莱德维尔、博伊西、斯内克河峡谷等地。但她从未停止过缅怀自己留在东海岸的文明生活。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: It's just a magnificent book, and Susan Burling Ward, who he's writing about, is just one of the most fully realized characters in American fiction that I have come across. And I actually made a new friend because of Wallace Stegner.
transcript.zh: 这是一本极其精彩的杰作，他笔下的苏珊·伯林·沃德是我在美国家小说中所读到过的塑造得最为丰满的人物之一。而且，我还因华莱士·斯特格纳结识了一位新朋友。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: A reader named Steven, who's fairly new to Beijing, he's here in a very interesting capacity that I don't feel at liberty to disclose just yet, but he, as it turns out, has a huge overlap with me in taste in books. And so he reached out, and we had lunch, and over a delicious meal of Yunnan mushrooms, we had this kind of Angle of Repose book club where we just dissected it, and it was just so much fun, just the two of us, it was insanely enjoyable.
transcript.zh: 一位名叫史蒂文的读者，刚到北京不久，他在这里的身份十分特别，我目前还不便透露。事实证明，他在阅读品味上与我有着极大的重合。于是他联系了我，我们一起吃了午饭。在一顿美味的云南菌子宴上，我们办了一场关于《驻膝之角》的两人读书会，深入剖析了这本书。只有我们两个人，但真的太开心、太尽兴了。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So thank you to Steven, and I really look forward to the next one, if you're listening. And again, let me just remind everybody about Jessica's two interviews that you want to definitely check out. Those would have made my list of recommendations happily.
transcript.zh: 所以感谢史蒂文，如果你在听的话，我非常期待我们的下一次交流。此外，让我再次提醒大家关注 Jessica 推荐的那两场访谈，绝对值得一听。它们完全可以直接进入我的推荐清单。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So yeah, the Dan Kurtz-Phelan one in particular is just outstanding. And again, thank you both. I have learned so much from this piece. It's super important and super timely, one of the more important things to read ahead of the state visit that's coming up at the end of this month.
transcript.zh: 没错，尤其是与丹·库尔茨-费兰的那期尤为出色。再次感谢两位，我从你们这篇大作中学到了很多。这篇文章极其重要，也无比及时，是本月底国事访问前夕最值得研读的文章之一。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So thanks once again for all the time you've taken.
transcript.zh: 再次感谢二位拨冗参与。

transcript.speaker: Gloria Xiong
transcript.en: Always great to be here, Kaiser. Thanks.
transcript.zh: 非常高兴来做客，Kaiser，谢谢。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Thanks, Jessica. Thank you, Gloria.
transcript.zh: 谢谢 Jessica，谢谢 Gloria。
